Long’s Work on Agnostic Learning with {0, 1, ?}-valued Hypotheses. Long (2001) considered a very similar learning setting where the goal is to agnostically learn a class of {0, 1, ?}labelled hypotheses, where ? is thought of as “don’t know” and the 0/1-loss function ` is extended to {0, 1, ?}2 by setting `(?, y) = `(y, ?) = 1 for all y ∈ {0, 1, ?}. Long proved that agnostic learnability of a class H in his setting is characterized by the finiteness of the VC dimension of H. While this is similar to Theorem 3 here, there is a key difference between the definitions of agnostic learnability in Long’s work and here. In a nutshell, the definition here is more restrictive in the sense that every agnostic learning algorithm according to our definition is also an agnostic learner according to Long’s definition, but not vice versa. We discuss these differences in more detail when we define agnostic learnability in Section C.2. (See Definition 38, Lemma 39, and footnote 13.) It is interesting to note that the agnostic learning algorithm which Long uses is very different from the one used here and can be seen as some sort of a transductive empirical risk minimizer. We may also note that this learner achieves a suboptimal sample complexity proportional to 1/ε3 , rather than 1/ε2 as in Theorem 41. B. Data-Dependent Generalization Guarantees In this section we describe how one can view datadependent generalization bounds as Structural Risk Minimization over partial concept classes. Already in 1974, Vapnik and Chervonenkis (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1974b) showed that standard VC-dimensionbased bounds can be significantly improved in the case of linear classifiers that correctly classify the data with a large margin.
